opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest starting point is that nobody really knows yet what data will be valuable in five years, and that uncertainty should shape how the collaboration works. Right now there's a gold-rush feeling around human data for robotics: teleoperation, egocentric video, wearable capture, motion data. Companies are scaling up collection really fast, and the risk is that we end up with huge piles of data that are cheap to collect but don't actually transfer to the capabilities we care about.

So what research institutions can bring is the question of *why* certain data helps. In academia we have the freedom to run careful, sometimes slow experiments: ablations on data diversity versus quantity, on which modalities matter, on whether you need action labels or whether passive human video is enough, on how embodiment gaps between a human hand and a robot gripper affect transfer. Those studies are hard to justify inside a company that has a quarterly target, but they're exactly what tells you whether a dataset will still be useful once models and hardware change.

Companies, on the other hand, have the operational muscle: the scale, the logistics, the ability to deploy capture devices across thousands of homes or workplaces. Academics usually can't do that. So I see a natural loop. Labs propose hypotheses and small-scale evidence about what kinds of data matter. Companies test those at scale and report back what actually moves the needle. Then the research community refines the theory.

A couple of concrete things would make this work better. One is shared evaluation. If we don't agree on benchmarks and real-world tasks that measure downstream robot performance, every company will claim its data is the most valuable, and there's no way to check. The second is collecting data in a way that's future-proof: richer sensing than you think you need, good calibration, metadata, synchronized streams. Raw, well-documented data ages much better than data that's been processed for one particular model architecture. The third is openness, at least partially. Even if companies keep most of their data proprietary, releasing slices of it, or the collection protocols, lets researchers study it and builds trust.

And finally, I'd encourage both sides to stay humble about the bitter lesson. Sometimes the data we think is "low quality" turns out to be enormously valuable at scale, and sometimes carefully curated data turns out to be a bottleneck. The best way through that is a tight feedback loop between people asking the scientific questions and people who can actually collect at scale.

r001.rationale: The response describes researchers using data to test what makes it useful, while companies provide collection scale and test findings in practice. It also recommends sharing data or protocols so researchers can study them, conveying the complementary relationship.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. That's a question I think about a lot, because right now the two sides are mostly guessing at each other.

The honest answer is that nobody knows exactly what data will be valuable in five years. What we do know, from a robot learning perspective, is what has *not* aged well. Data collected on a single bespoke platform, in a single lab setup, with a very narrow task distribution tends to lose value quickly, because the hardware changes, the sensors change, and the policy architectures change. So the first thing I'd push for is that collection companies and research groups agree on what makes data robust to those shifts, rather than trying to predict the exact tasks people will care about.

Concretely, I think that means a few things. One is prioritizing diversity over volume. Ten thousand demonstrations of the same pick-and-place in the same kitchen are worth far less than a thousand demonstrations across many objects, lighting conditions, and scene layouts. Research institutions are actually pretty good at characterizing that distribution, and companies are good at executing at scale, so that's a natural division of labor.

Another is being disciplined about what gets recorded alongside the demonstration itself. Raw proprioception, calibrated camera intrinsics and extrinsics, timestamps, language annotations, failure cases, even the operator's hesitation. Much of what makes a dataset useful later is metadata that seemed boring at collection time. Researchers should be in the room to say, "please don't throw that away."

And then there's the feedback loop. The most productive collaborations I've seen are the ones where the lab trains models on an early batch, finds out where the policies break, and that directly reshapes the next round of collection. It's less a handoff and more a continuous conversation. If a company collects a year's worth of data and only then asks the research community whether it's useful, that's a very expensive way to find out the answer is "partly."

I'd also say we should be a bit humble about human data specifically. Teleoperation is the dominant source right now, but a lot of the long-term value may come from mixing it with simulation, with egocentric human video, and with autonomously collected robot experience. So the question is not just "which human data is valuable," but "which human data is the piece that those other sources can't provide." Usually that's contact-rich manipulation, recovery from failures, and the subtle strategy choices people make that are hard to script.

So, if I had to boil it down: agree on standards for diversity and metadata, build the loop so models trained on the data inform collection within weeks rather than years, and treat human demonstrations as the scarce, high-value component of a larger data ecosystem rather than the whole thing.

r001.rationale: The response describes researchers using early data batches to train models and identify failures, while collection companies execute and adjust collection based on that feedback. This communicates complementary needs and roles.

astra-6.text:
I think it has to be a close, ongoing collaboration, because we don’t yet know exactly what human data will be most useful in the long term. Research institutions can help identify what current models are missing and design experiments to test whether a particular kind of data actually helps. Collection companies can tell us what’s feasible to capture reliably and at scale.

The important thing is to build a feedback loop. Before collecting a huge dataset, collect a smaller amount, train on it, and evaluate whether it improves the capabilities we care about—especially on tasks and environments the model hasn’t seen before. Then use those results to guide the next round of collection.

I’d also want to preserve enough context that the data remains useful as methods change: what the person was trying to do, what they observed, and what happened when something went wrong. We should be developing that understanding together, rather than assuming that more hours of data will automatically translate into more capability.

r001.rationale: The response describes complementary roles: research institutions identify model gaps and test what data helps, while collection companies contribute feasibility and scale information; shared evaluation results guide future collection.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it has to be a much tighter feedback loop. Research institutions are exploring what the next generation of models will need, while data collection companies understand what you can actually collect reliably and at scale. Neither side can determine the long-term value of data on its own.

So I would start with smaller, shared experiments. Collect a dataset around a particular capability, train on it, and evaluate whether that capability improves—especially on tasks or environments the model hasn’t seen before. Then use those results to guide the next round of collection. Otherwise, you can spend a lot of money collecting something that looks diverse but doesn’t actually help the model generalize.

And I think the important thing is to share what was learned, including the failures. Which kinds of variation mattered? What information was missing? How much did the quality of the collection affect the result? Over time, that gives us a more grounded way to decide what’s worth collecting, even as the models change.

r001.rationale: The response says research institutions explore what future models will need, while data-collection companies know what can be collected reliably at scale. It adds that neither can determine long-term value alone and proposes shared experiments to assess usefulness.
